logline: Blind lawyer Matt Murdock fights crime in Hell's Kitchen by day and as the vigilante Daredevil by night - Marvel and Netflix's grittiest collaboration, ended by cancellation in 2018 before its story was done.

renewal.note: Netflix cancelled the series November 29, 2018, after three seasons, as part of its broader wind-down of the Marvel TV partnership. Charlie Cox reprised the role in the MCU proper; Daredevil: Born Again (2025) is a separate entry.

bollymeter.basis: A 99% Rotten Tomatoes score from 72 critics is the highest of the Netflix Marvel era and among the highest any superhero TV series has recorded. Season 1 redefined what a comic-book adaptation could achieve: street-level brutality, a villain (Kingpin) with genuine psychological complexity, and fight choreography that set a new industry benchmark.

pull_quotes.text: Marvel has shrewdly expanded its portfolio, and Netflix has upped its must-have quotient with a fiercely loyal segment of consumers.

seasons.review_body: Released April 10, 2015, Daredevil Season 1 is a defining high point of the Netflix Marvel era and a standout superhero production, holding 99 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 72 reviews, an 8.6 on IMDb, and a 93 percent audience approval on Rotten Tomatoes. Two achievements help define its impact: the corridor fight in Episode 2, a single-take brawl that stands out as a landmark action sequence in superhero television, and Vincent D’Onofrio’s Kingpin, shaped with the complexity and weight of a prestige drama antagonist rather than a simple comic-book obstacle. The series proves that Marvel’s darker street-level characters can sustain a tonal register closer to The Wire than to the Avengers films. Charlie Cox’s physically committed lead performance grounds the mythology in something recognisably human.

episode_reviews.title: Cut Man
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode that announced this was a different kind of superhero show. The hallway sequence - Matt Murdock, exhausted and beaten, fighting through a corridor of armed men in a single unbroken take - became one of the most referenced pieces of action television of the decade. The episode surrounding it is equally strong: the structure alternates past and present to explain why Murdock keeps fighting despite the cost.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The corridor. One take. No cuts. A man who cannot see, winning through sheer refusal to stop.

episode_reviews.title: Daredevil
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale delivers on every narrative thread - Murdock and Fisk converge in a rooftop confrontation and a street-level final battle that earns the costume's debut without fan-service excess. The Kingpin's final scene reframes him as something genuinely terrifying in defeat, setting up a villain whose story clearly has further to run.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The red suit appears for the first time. After thirteen episodes of black, it lands exactly as hard as the show intended.

bollymeter.basis: An 81% Rotten Tomatoes score from 57 critics reflects a season with two genuinely excellent halves - the Punisher arc and the Elektra arc - that never fully cohere. Jon Bernthal's Punisher is a franchise-launching performance; the Hand mythology that bookends the season is the show's weakest ingredient.

seasons.review_body: Season 2, released March 18, 2016, introduced Frank Castle, also known as the Punisher, and Elektra in the same season, a bold structural choice that brings its own strain. The Punisher arc, especially the rooftop debate about vigilante ethics between the Punisher and Daredevil, frames the season at a similar level of quality to Season 1. Jon Bernthal’s performance stands out and set up a spin-off series. By contrast, the Elektra storyline and the Hand mythology register as the weaker thread, with conspiratorial scaffolding that the show has difficulty turning into sustained momentum. The Rotten Tomatoes figure of 81 percent based on 57 critics does not erase the visible quality gap between the season’s two halves. Audience scores stay at 89 percent, showing a continued pull of the action even as the plotting loses traction.
seasons.season_over_season: Trades the focused villain architecture of Season 1 for two competing antagonist arcs; the Punisher half matches the original's quality, the Hand mythology does not.

bollymeter.basis: A 97% Rotten Tomatoes score from 67 critics put Season 3 level with the debut - a remarkable recovery after the Defenders crossover and Season 2's structural issues. The return of Kingpin and Bullseye gave the season two credible villains; the one-take prison fight surpassed even Episode 2 of Season 1 in critical estimation.

seasons.review_body: Released October 19, 2018, Season 3 arrives as the send-off the Netflix Marvel era deserved rather than an officially planned conclusion. The season's central achievement is Episode 4's prison brawl, an unbroken action sequence that moves prison, corridor by corridor, room by room, with a wider scope than the Season 1 hallway set-piece and ranked among the finest single action sequences in television. Vincent D'Onofrio's Kingpin returns as the season's fulcrum, and the show strips Murdock down to his lowest point before its final arc. Netflix cancelled the series six weeks after the season's release. The ending works as an accidental series finale, offering enough resolution to stand on its own.
seasons.season_over_season: A complete rehabilitation after Season 2's structural sprawl - tighter villain architecture, the series' most extraordinary action sequence, and Charlie Cox's best performance of the run.
